newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS - GREEK BANKERS CALMER ON NEW INTERBANK TAX.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - GREEK BANKERS CALMER ON NEW INTERBANK TAX.

text.p: After initial upheaval, Greece's bankers on Wednesday calmed down concerning a new tax on net income from interbank deals, which the socialist government plans from next January.
But bankers expressed apprehension that the combined effect of planned new taxes on government T-bills and bonds as well as the interbank deals would push premiums higher.

The government's outline of its plans for the 1997 budget, due this month, has been set against a backdrop of anxiety over taxes and a settlement scandal at the Athens bourse which closed operations for part of last week.
The finance ministry said on Tuesday it would tax net income from interbank deals, from January 1, as other bank income.
Before the announcement, confusion over what the government was planning, and fears of a 15 percent withholding tax, halted interbank trade for periods over one month.
"I just hope the finance ministry officials will learn their lesson from this episode and stop surprising the market in the future," said a senior dealer who expressed relief over the outcome.

Because banks will pay taxes on net interest income from interbank transactions in 1998 for fiscal 1997, the finance ministry decided to raise the 1997 income tax prepayment of banks to 60 percent from 50 percent.
"It is a positive development in the sense that the (new) tax is market neutral," said Harris Makkas, deputy general manager and treasurer at Bank of America, Athens.
"My only apprehension is that new taxes and the recent bourse crisis will be reflected in policy uncertainty premiums," he added.
Higher risk premiums might keep interest rates slightly higher than they should be in the short-term and it might take some time before they are erased, said Makkas.
"It's positive that the confusion over the interbank tax is over and the market is back to trading normally," Mike Papparis, treasurer of Midland Bank, Athens, said.
The national economy ministry also announced on Tuesday that it will impose a 7.5 percent tax on T-bills and bonds issued after January 1.
The new tax measures coincide with final work on the 1997 budget, which must go to parliament by the end of the month.
Other bankers said the impact of the new tax will be minimal although it was biased against interbank placements.

"The new tax will not affect interest rates until year-end and might have a marginal effect after January 1 depending on whether the central bank expands its open market operations," said a state bank dealer.
"Under the new tax regime, the central bank will have to inject liquidity into the system, especially in periods of stress and large auctions, more often than before," said the state bank dealer.

The dealer added that the new tax would penalise players who were long and could affect the dividend policy of large banks that used to put their previously tax-free net interest from interbank dealings into retained earnings.

"The current tax regime is biased in favour of interbank placements and the new tax certainly works the other way, creating disincentives for interbank deals," another senior dealer said. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
